faqs.q: Do I need flood insurance in Baldwin County?
faqs.a: Flood insurance is generally required for a property in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area (a high-risk zone such as AE or VE) with a federally backed mortgage. Your lender may also require it outside a high-risk zone. When no one requires it, the choice is yours. Still, coastal Baldwin County communities like Gulf Shores and Orange Beach see flood damage well beyond official flood-zone lines. Many homeowners carry it either way. FEMA's FloodSmart site explains flood insurance eligibility.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover flooding?
faqs.a: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood damage. Flood coverage is generally purchased separately, through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) or a private carrier. Your policy's terms decide what is covered.

faqs.q: What does NFIP flood insurance cover in Alabama?
faqs.a: The National Flood Insurance Program covers direct physical damage from flooding to your building and, if selected, its contents, up to the program's coverage limits. It's a separate policy from your homeowners insurance, which excludes flood entirely.

faqs.q: What affects flood insurance rates in Alabama and Baldwin County?
faqs.a: NFIP flood policies are priced under FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 method, which looks at the individual home rather than relying only on its flood zone. Factors include the home's distance to the coast or other water and the kinds of flooding that affect the area. They also include the home's elevation, foundation type and rebuilding cost, plus the coverage and deductible chosen. Private flood carriers set their prices their own way. We can show what applies to a specific address.

faqs.q: How do I find out my FEMA flood zone in Baldwin County?
faqs.a: Baldwin County's FEMA flood map shows the zone for every address. We look up your zone as part of your quote, along with your elevation if you have a certificate on file.

faqs.q: What's an elevation certificate and do I need one for flood insurance?
faqs.a: An elevation certificate, prepared by a licensed surveyor, documents how high your home sits relative to the base flood elevation for your zone. It can affect your flood insurance rate, and some flood zones require one. If you don't have one, we can point you toward how to get it.

faqs.q: Can I get flood insurance through a private carrier instead of NFIP?
faqs.a: Yes, several private carriers write flood coverage for coastal Alabama property as an alternative to NFIP, sometimes with different limits or pricing. We'll show you what's available for your address.

faqs.q: Can I bundle homeowners and flood insurance together?
faqs.a: Flood coverage is written as a separate policy from your homeowners policy, but we can quote and manage both together so you're working with one agent instead of two.

faqs.q: How fast can I get flood coverage?
faqs.a: NFIP policies typically have a 30-day waiting period before coverage takes effect, with some exceptions such as a new mortgage closing. Private flood policies can sometimes bind faster. We'll walk you through the timing for your situation.

faqs.q: What should I do if my home floods?
faqs.a: Once it is safe to go inside, take photos and video of the water line and the damage, and keep receipts for cleanup and repairs. Report the damage to your flood insurance carrier as soon as you can, since NFIP policies set deadlines for sending proof of loss. Before throwing out damaged items, photograph them and note what they are, because the carrier may ask for details or samples, such as a piece of carpet. Brian can help you find your carrier's claim contact. See the after-the-storm guide.

faqs.q: Does flood insurance have to be escrowed with my mortgage?
faqs.a: If your mortgage requires flood insurance, federal rules generally require your lender to collect the premium through your escrow account, along with your property taxes and homeowners insurance. Some loans are exceptions, such as certain home equity lines and loans from smaller lenders. Your lender decides how yours is handled, and we can send them the policy details they need.

faqs.q: Does flood insurance cover a burst pipe or water backing up from a drain?
faqs.a: Usually not. Flood insurance is for water that comes from outside, such as rising water or storm surge covering the ground around your home. A burst pipe is a homeowners policy question, and drain or sewer backup is generally a flood claim only when a flood causes it; many homeowners policies offer a separate water backup endorsement. What a policy covers always depends on its terms.

faqs.q: Can the seller's flood policy transfer to me when I buy a home in Fairhope?
faqs.a: Often, yes. An NFIP policy on a building can generally be transferred from the seller to the buyer at closing, and taking it over can keep the policy's current rating instead of starting fresh. Contents-only policies can't be transferred, and private flood policies follow their own rules, so it's worth asking early in your purchase.

faqs.q: Can I cancel my flood insurance?
faqs.a: NFIP flood policies can be cancelled only for reasons FEMA allows, such as selling the home or no longer having a lender that requires the coverage. In those cases part of the premium may be refunded, though fees are not. Before dropping flood coverage, keep in mind that homeowners insurance excludes flood and a new NFIP policy usually has a 30-day waiting period.

faqs.q: Can I get flood insurance for a mobile or manufactured home?
faqs.a: Yes. The NFIP can cover a manufactured home that sits on a permanent foundation and is anchored the way FEMA requires, and some private carriers write them as well. Tell us how your home is set up and anchored, and we'll check which options fit.

sections.h: What Midwest buyers look for in Baldwin County
p: Baldwin County is one of the fastest growing counties in Alabama. The U.S. Census Bureau estimates it grew from 231,767 residents in April 2020 to 267,761 in July 2025, about 15.5 percent. Brian works with buyers relocating from across the Midwest, along with some from New York, and they often arrive with a similar wish list:
Mild winters and a longer outdoor season. No snow shovel, more time on the bay, the beach, the golf course or the boat.
Lower property taxes. Alabama property taxes are among the lowest in the country, and owner-occupants can apply for a homestead exemption through the Baldwin County Revenue Commission.

Small-town character. Walkable downtowns and established neighborhoods in Fairhope and Daphne, the first stop for many relocating buyers, plus quieter communities in Silverhill, Magnolia Springs and Loxley.
Newer construction. Planned neighborhoods in Foley, Spanish Fort and Robertsdale, often with HOAs, sidewalks and community pools.
Water access. Beach homes and condos in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, and bayfront, river and canal homes along Mobile Bay, sometimes as a second home before a full move.
Room for toys. Space and coverage for a boat, golf cart, RV or a second vehicle for visiting family.

Each of those choices affects insurance. Distance from the water, elevation, roof type and age, and whether a home is a primary residence, second home or condo all change which carriers can write the policy and how it is built.

sections.h: Plan for a hurricane deductible
p: Most Gulf Coast homeowners policies have a separate deductible for hurricane or named-storm damage, as the policy defines it.
It is often a percentage of the dwelling coverage instead of a flat amount, so it can be far larger than the deductible on a typical Midwest policy.
Ask how it is calculated, when it applies, and what other deductible options the carrier offers. See hurricane deductibles explained.

sections.h: Treat flood as its own policy
p: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood. Flood is usually written separately through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood carrier.
Lenders generally require it for federally backed loans on homes in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area. Outside those zones it is optional, and many buyers still consider it.

NFIP policies generally have a 30-day waiting period, with some exceptions such as coverage bought with a new loan. Ask the seller for an elevation certificate if one exists. More on the flood insurance page.

sections.h: Know how wind is covered near the coast
p: In coastal Baldwin and Mobile counties, some homes have wind and hail coverage written on a separate policy from the rest of the homeowners coverage.

The Alabama Insurance Underwriting Association, the state's wind pool, writes wind coverage for eligible properties south of the 31st parallel in Baldwin and Mobile counties when the regular market does not.
When a home needs two or three policies (homeowners, wind and flood), it helps to have one agent who sees how they fit together.

sections.h: Look at the roof first
p: Roof age, material and condition shape which carriers will write a coastal home. A newer roof can open more options.

A FORTIFIED designation from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety qualifies a home for discounts on the wind portion of the premium from admitted Alabama carriers, under Alabama Department of Insurance rules.

The Strengthen Alabama Homes program offers grants toward a FORTIFIED Roof for eligible owner-occupied homes, subject to program rules and funding. If the home already has a FORTIFIED certificate, ask the seller for a copy.

sections.h: Get quotes before you are committed
p: Request quotes during your inspection or due diligence period, not the week of closing. Your lender will need proof of insurance before closing.
During hurricane season, carriers may pause new policies when a storm threatens the Gulf, which can delay a closing that waited too long.

Share the inspection report, roof age, any wind mitigation or FORTIFIED paperwork, and the flood zone with your agent. Brian also holds an International Code Council residential building inspector certification, which helps him read those reports with you.

sections.h: Move your cars, boat and golf cart over too
p: Alabama gives new residents 30 days from the date a vehicle enters the state to title and register it, and the vehicle must have Alabama liability insurance first.
Boats, golf carts and RVs each need their own coverage conversation. See auto, boat and RV insurance.

sections.h: Do homes in Baldwin County have basements?
p: Basements are uncommon on the Alabama Gulf Coast because of the high water table and low elevation, and many coastal homes are built on raised foundations or pilings. sections.h: Midwest vs. Alabama insurance at a glance
p: Every state and every policy is different, so treat this as a map of what usually changes, not a description of any one policy.

sections.h: Home insurance: what changes when you move south
p: From the house you are selling to the one you are buying, these are the home insurance points Midwest families ask about most.

sections.h: Your Midwest homeowners policy stays with that house
p: A homeowners policy is written for one property in one state. It does not move with you, even if your company also writes policies in Alabama.
Plan for a new Alabama policy that starts on your closing date, and keep your Midwest policy in force until that home is sold and closed.
If your current company writes in Alabama, it is worth asking about, but coastal availability varies by carrier and by address, so it helps to compare options.

sections.h: Protect the house you are leaving
p: Many homeowners policies limit certain coverages once a home has been vacant for a stretch of time. The policy wording sets how long that is, so check yours before you move out.
If your Midwest home will sit empty while it is listed, tell your current agent and ask whether you need a vacancy endorsement or a vacant dwelling policy.
Winterize the plumbing and keep the heat on if the house will sit through a northern winter. A burst pipe in an empty house is a common and avoidable claim.

sections.h: Know how your belongings are covered on the road
p: Homeowners policies often extend limited coverage to personal property while it is away from the home, subject to the policy's terms and limits.
Moving companies offer valuation options, such as released value or full value protection. Valuation is the mover's liability, not insurance, so read what each option pays.
If you store belongings in a storage unit between homes, ask how your policy treats property in storage and for how long.

sections.h: Do the hurricane deductible math before you choose
p: Most Gulf Coast homeowners policies use a separate deductible for hurricane or named-storm damage, as the policy defines it.

It is often a percentage of your dwelling coverage, rather than the flat-dollar deductible many Midwest homeowners are used to. For example, a 2 percent deductible on a home insured for 400,000 dollars is 8,000 dollars.
Ask how the deductible is calculated, when it applies, and what other options the carrier offers, then plan your savings around the number you choose.

sections.h: Expect wind and flood to be separate conversations
p: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood. Flood is usually its own policy through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood carrier, and NFIP policies generally have a 30-day waiting period, with some exceptions such as coverage bought with a new loan.
Some homes south of the 31st parallel in Baldwin and Mobile counties have wind and hail written on a separate policy, sometimes through the Alabama Insurance Underwriting Association.
Our Moving to Baldwin County guide and flood insurance page go deeper on both.

sections.h: Look at the roof the way an Alabama carrier will
p: Roof age, material, shape and condition shape which carriers will write a coastal home. In the Midwest the roof conversation is usually about hail; here it is about wind.

A FORTIFIED designation from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety qualifies a home for discounts on the wind portion of the premium from admitted Alabama carriers, under Alabama Department of Insurance rules.
The Strengthen Alabama Homes program offers grants toward a FORTIFIED Roof for eligible owner-occupied homes, subject to program rules and funding.

sections.h: Keeping a home up north? Settle which one is primary
p: Many Midwest families winter on the Gulf Coast before moving full time. The home you live in most of the year is usually your primary residence, and the other is a secondary or seasonal home, which can change the policy form and the options available.
Seasonal homes sit empty for months. Ask how each policy treats unoccupied periods, and consider an automatic water shut-off valve on the house you are away from.
If you plan to rent a Gulf Shores or Orange Beach home or condo to vacationers, tell your agent. Short-term rentals usually need different coverage than a home you live in.

sections.h: Auto insurance: what changes when you register in Alabama
p: Alabama's auto rules differ from most of the Midwest in a few ways that are worth understanding before you choose limits.

sections.h: Alabama is an at-fault state, with no PIP requirement
p: In Alabama, the driver who causes an accident is generally responsible for the other people's injuries and damage, and that driver's liability insurance is where those claims usually go first.

Alabama does not require personal injury protection (PIP). Coming from Michigan, Minnesota, Kansas or North Dakota, you will not find the no-fault medical benefits you are used to on an Alabama policy.

Coverage that can help with your own injuries in Alabama includes medical payments coverage (optional), uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, and your health insurance, each subject to its own terms.

sections.h: Choose liability limits for what you own, not just the minimum
p: Alabama's minimum liability limits are 25/50/25: 25,000 dollars for bodily injury to one person, 50,000 for all bodily injury in one accident, and 25,000 for property damage.
Minimums are the legal floor. Drivers who own a home or have savings often choose higher limits, and some add a personal umbrella policy on top.
If you carried higher limits in the Midwest, bring your current declarations page so your Alabama quote can start from the same place.

sections.h: Keep uninsured motorist coverage in view
p: Under Alabama law, auto liability policies include uninsured motorist coverage unless the named insured rejects it. Carriers usually ask for a signed rejection form.
Uninsured motorist coverage is designed to help when the at-fault driver has no insurance, or, for underinsured coverage, not enough insurance for your injuries, subject to the policy's terms.
Many drivers choose uninsured motorist limits that match their liability limits. Ask your agent to show you both side by side.

sections.h: Understand why Alabama drivers look closely at their own coverage
p: Alabama is one of a few states that still follow contributory negligence. Under that rule, a person found even slightly at fault for an accident may be barred from recovering damages from the other driver.
That is one reason many Alabama drivers pay close attention to coverages that do not depend on the other driver, such as collision, medical payments and uninsured motorist coverage.
This is general information, not legal advice. For questions about a specific accident, talk with an Alabama attorney.

sections.h: Register within 30 days, with Alabama insurance first
p: New residents have 30 days from the date a vehicle enters Alabama to title and register it, and the vehicle must have Alabama liability insurance before it can be registered.
Alabama checks insurance electronically through the Online Insurance Verification System (OIVS) when plates are issued and renewed, so the policy needs to be active and on the right vehicle.
The Alabama Law Enforcement Agency (ALEA) lets new residents drive on a valid license from their prior state for 30 days. Out-of-state license transfers are handled at an ALEA office.

sections.h: Start the Alabama auto policy before you cancel the old one
p: Auto rates are based in part on where the car is garaged, so the policy should change to Alabama when the cars do.
Have the Alabama policy start the day you arrive, then cancel the Midwest policy effective the same day. Avoid a gap in coverage, even for a day.
Let your old company know your move date. Most will refund unused premium on a cancelled policy, subject to the policy's terms.

sections.h: Know what covers your car in a hurricane
p: Flood and wind damage to a car is generally handled under comprehensive coverage on the auto policy, not under a flood or homeowners policy.
If your car is paid off and you dropped comprehensive up north, revisit that choice on the Gulf Coast.
Carriers may pause new policies and coverage increases when a storm threatens the Gulf, so make changes well before hurricane season gets busy.

sections.h: Bring the boat, golf cart and RV into the plan
p: Boats, golf carts, motorcycles and RVs each need their own coverage conversation, and Gulf Coast use (salt water, storm season, storage) can change it.
See auto, motorcycle, boat and RV insurance for what Brian can quote.

faqs.q: Will my Midwest home and auto insurance cover me after I move to Alabama?
faqs.a: Not for long. A homeowners policy is written for one property, so your new Alabama home needs its own policy starting on your closing date. Auto policies are rated by the state and address where the car is garaged, so you will need an Alabama auto policy once you move, and Alabama requires Alabama liability insurance before you can register the vehicle. Keep the Midwest policies in force until the new ones start.

faqs.q: Is Alabama a no-fault state for car insurance?
faqs.a: No. Alabama is an at-fault (tort) state. The driver who causes an accident is generally responsible for the resulting injuries and damage, and Alabama does not require personal injury protection (PIP). In the Midwest, Michigan, Minnesota, Kansas and North Dakota use no-fault systems, so drivers from those states will notice the biggest change.

faqs.q: I am moving from Michigan. What happens to my PIP coverage in Alabama?
faqs.a: Michigan's no-fault PIP benefits do not carry over to an Alabama policy, because Alabama does not use a no-fault system. On an Alabama policy, injuries to you and your passengers are typically addressed through the at-fault driver's liability coverage, your own medical payments coverage if you choose it, uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, and your health insurance, each subject to its own terms. Review those choices carefully when you set up your Alabama policy.

faqs.q: What are the minimum auto insurance requirements in Alabama?
faqs.a: Alabama requires liability coverage of at least 25/50/25: 25,000 dollars for bodily injury to one person, 50,000 dollars for all bodily injury in one accident, and 25,000 dollars for property damage. These are minimums, and many drivers choose higher limits to protect their home and savings.

faqs.q: Do I need uninsured motorist coverage in Alabama?
faqs.a: Alabama law requires auto liability policies to include uninsured motorist coverage unless the named insured rejects it. Carriers usually ask for a signed rejection form. It is designed to help with your injuries when the at-fault driver has no insurance or not enough, subject to the policy's terms. Many drivers choose uninsured motorist limits that match their liability limits.

faqs.q: How long do I have to register my car and change my license after moving to Alabama?
faqs.a: New residents have 30 days from the date a vehicle enters Alabama to title and register it, and the vehicle must be covered by Alabama liability insurance first. The Alabama Law Enforcement Agency also allows new residents to drive on a valid license from their previous state for 30 days after becoming a resident.

faqs.q: Why is home insurance on the Alabama coast set up differently than in the Midwest?
faqs.a: Because the main risk is different. Midwest policies are built around hail, tornadoes, freezing and snow, while Gulf Coast policies are built around hurricanes. That is why coastal Alabama homes often have a separate hurricane or named-storm deductible, a separate flood policy, and sometimes a separate wind policy, and why roof age, elevation and flood zone matter so much to carriers.

faqs.q: Do I still need to think about hail and tornadoes in Alabama?
faqs.a: Yes. Alabama has tornadoes and hail too, including along the Gulf Coast, so wind and hail coverage still matter on every home. The difference near the coast is the added hurricane risk, which is why the hurricane or named-storm deductible gets so much attention here.

faqs.q: How do I insure my Midwest house while it is for sale and empty?
faqs.a: Tell your current agent when the house will be vacant. Many homeowners policies limit certain coverages after a home has been vacant for a period of time, and the policy wording sets how long that is. Your agent can tell you whether you need a vacancy endorsement or a vacant dwelling policy until the home sells.

faqs.q: Are my belongings covered while they are being moved?
faqs.a: Homeowners policies often provide limited coverage for personal property away from the home, subject to the policy's terms and limits. The moving company's valuation options, such as released value or full value protection, describe the mover's liability and are not insurance. Ask your agent how your policy treats items in transit and in storage before moving day.

faqs.q: Does flood insurance cover my car in a hurricane?
faqs.a: No. A flood insurance policy covers buildings and their contents, not vehicles. Flood and wind damage to a car is generally covered under the comprehensive part of an auto policy, subject to its terms, so drivers on the Gulf Coast often keep comprehensive even on a paid-off car.

faqs.q: Can I keep my insurance company when I move to Alabama?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If your current company writes policies in Alabama, it can usually issue new Alabama policies, but they are new policies under Alabama rules and rates, and coastal home availability varies by carrier and address. An independent agent can compare that option with other carriers for the same property.

sections.h: How the math works
p: A percentage deductible is figured from the dwelling coverage limit (Coverage A) on your declarations page, not from the size of the claim. On an AIUA wind policy, the percentage is applied to the structure's total insurable value, which can differ from the limit. As an illustration only:
2 percent of $300,000 in dwelling coverage is a $6,000 hurricane deductible.
5 percent of the same $300,000 is a $15,000 hurricane deductible.
Your own figure depends on your dwelling limit and the percentage on your policy. Because the deductible grows with the dwelling limit, it also grows when a policy's coverage is increased at renewal.

sections.h: What triggers it
p: Each policy defines when the hurricane or named-storm deductible applies. Many tie it to a hurricane or tropical storm named by the National Hurricane Center, sometimes for a set period before and after the storm.
Triggers vary by carrier, so read the definition on your own policy or ask your agent to point it out.

sections.h: How it differs from your other deductibles
p: Your all-other-perils deductible applies to covered losses like a kitchen fire or theft. It is usually a flat amount.
Some policies also have a separate wind/hail deductible for wind or hail damage from storms that are not named.
Flood is generally excluded from homeowners policies and written separately, and a flood policy has its own deductible. See flood insurance.

sections.h: When wind is on a separate policy
p: For some coastal homes, wind and hail are excluded from the homeowners policy and written on a separate wind policy, sometimes called windstorm insurance or a wind-only policy, sometimes through the Alabama Insurance Underwriting Association. See wind insurance and the AIUA.
In that case the named-storm deductible sits on the wind policy, so ask about the deductible on each policy.

sections.h: Ways to plan for it
p: Ask what deductible options the carrier offers. A lower deductible generally means a higher premium, and a higher one generally means a lower premium.
Set aside savings or another financial cushion that could cover the deductible if a storm hits.

A FORTIFIED designation qualifies a home for discounts on the wind portion of the premium from admitted Alabama carriers, under Alabama Department of Insurance rules. The Strengthen Alabama Homes program offers grants toward a FORTIFIED Roof for eligible owner-occupied homes, subject to program rules and funding. See FORTIFIED roofs explained.
Photograph your home and belongings before the season starts. See the hurricane preparedness checklist and the after-the-storm guide.

sections.h: Hurricane deductibles in coastal areas
p: Hurricane deductibles are common on property insurance in coastal states along the Gulf and Atlantic, including Alabama, Mississippi and Florida. Each state sets its own rules, and each insurer writes its own policy terms.

Homes in coastal areas such as south Baldwin County often have higher percentages or fewer deductible options than homes farther inland, depending on the insurer and the home's distance from the water.
There is usually no separate hurricane insurance policy. Wind damage from hurricanes is covered by the homeowners or wind policy, subject to its terms, and flood damage by a flood policy.
If you have a mortgage, the lender may set a maximum deductible as a condition of the loan. Check your loan documents before choosing a higher percentage.

sections.h: How it applies to a hurricane claim
p: After hurricanes and named storms, insurers adjust the covered wind damage and subtract the hurricane deductible from what they pay on the claim.

Flood claims go to the flood insurer and use the flood policy's own deductible. See the after-the-storm guide.

sections.h: What is a hurricane deductible in Alabama?
p: A hurricane deductible is a separate deductible on many Alabama Gulf Coast homeowners and wind policies that applies to damage from a hurricane or named storm, as the policy defines it. It is often a percentage of the home's dwelling coverage rather than a flat amount, so it can be larger than the policy's regular deductible.

sections.h: How is a hurricane deductible calculated?
p: A percentage hurricane deductible is calculated from the dwelling coverage limit on the declarations page, not from the amount of the claim. On an AIUA wind policy, the percentage is applied to the structure's total insurable value, which can differ from the limit. For example, a 2 percent deductible on a home with 300,000 in dwelling coverage would be 6,000. The exact figure depends on the policy's dwelling limit and percentage.

sections.h: Does the hurricane deductible apply to flood damage?
p: No. Flood is generally excluded from homeowners policies and written on a separate flood policy, which has its own deductible. The hurricane deductible on a homeowners or wind policy applies to covered wind damage from a hurricane or named storm, subject to the policy's terms.

sections.h: Can I choose a lower hurricane deductible?
p: Many carriers offer more than one hurricane deductible option, and the choices depend on the carrier, the home's location and underwriting. A lower deductible generally means a higher premium. A licensed agent can show the options available for a specific home.

sections.h: Does a FORTIFIED roof change my hurricane deductible?
p: Under Alabama Department of Insurance rules, a FORTIFIED designation qualifies a home for discounts on the wind portion of the premium from admitted Alabama carriers. Whether it also changes deductible options depends on the carrier. Ask your agent what a FORTIFIED certificate would change for your policy.

sections.h: Is a hurricane deductible the same as a wind and hail deductible?
p: No. Many Alabama Gulf Coast policies have both. The hurricane or named-storm deductible applies to wind damage from a storm that meets the policy's definition, such as a storm named by the National Hurricane Center. A separate wind or hail deductible, when a policy has one, applies to wind or hail damage from other storms, such as a severe thunderstorm. Which deductible applies to a loss depends on the policy's terms.

sections.h: How do I choose a hurricane deductible percentage?
p: It depends on how much you could comfortably pay yourself after a storm and on the options the carrier offers for your home. A higher percentage generally means a lower premium but a larger share of a covered loss paid out of pocket. A practical step is to work out each option in dollars from the dwelling limit on your declarations page and compare it with the savings you could set aside. A licensed agent can show the options available for a specific home.

sections.h: Does a hurricane deductible apply once per year or to each storm?
p: It depends on the policy. Some policies apply the hurricane deductible on a calendar-year basis, which can affect what a homeowner pays if more than one named storm damages the home in the same year. Others apply it to each storm. The policy's terms spell out how a second storm in the same season is handled, so it is worth asking before hurricane season begins.

sections.h: How long does a hurricane deductible apply?
p: Each policy defines its own time window. Many start it when the National Hurricane Center, part of the National Weather Service, issues a hurricane watch or warning and end it a set number of hours after the watch or warning ends. Damage from the storm during that window falls under the hurricane deductible, subject to the policy's terms. The exact start, end and area are written in the policy.

sections.h: What is a hurricane deductible endorsement?
p: An endorsement is a form added to an insurance policy that changes or adds to its terms. A hurricane or named-storm deductible endorsement is the form that sets the hurricane deductible, including the percentage or amount, what triggers it and how long it applies. It is often listed by form number on the declarations page, alongside the deductible itself.

sections.h: How Gulf Shores condo insurance fits with the HOA master policy
p: The HOA master policy generally covers the building's structure and common areas, such as hallways, elevators and pools. Inside the units, associations draw the line in different ways. Three common setups:
Bare walls. The HOA insures the building structure. The owner insures nearly everything inside the unit, such as flooring, cabinets, fixtures and built-in appliances.
Original specifications. The HOA includes the unit's original interior finishes, and the owner insures upgrades and improvements made since.
All-in. The HOA includes interior finishes and improvements, and the owner mainly insures belongings and personal liability.
The condo documents and the master policy decide which setup applies. Ask the HOA or management company for the declarations page and the bylaws section on insurance.

sections.h: Coverage for the unit's interior
p: An HO-6 can include dwelling coverage for the parts of the unit the owner is responsible for under the condo documents.

An HO-6 can help with damage from covered causes such as fire, smoke, theft and burst pipes, subject to the policy's terms.

An HO-6 typically also includes personal property coverage for your belongings. Personal liability coverage can help if someone is injured in your unit. Loss of use can help with living costs if a covered loss makes the unit unlivable. Each is subject to the policy's limits and terms.

sections.h: Loss assessment coverage

sections.h: Flood for condos

sections.h: Why a rental needs a different policy
p: Homeowners policies are built for a home the owner lives in. Once someone else lives there or pays to stay there, the risks change, and so do the questions a carrier asks. Three common setups:

sections.h: Why townhouses are confusing to insure
p: "Townhouse" describes the look of a building: attached homes with shared walls. It does not say who owns what. Insurance follows ownership, so the same row of homes can be set up in different ways:
You own the building and the lot. The HOA handles common areas. Usually insured on a homeowners policy.
The community is a condominium. The association insures the buildings on a master policy. Usually insured on a condo policy.
Some communities split it differently, for example the association insures the roofs and exterior while owners insure the rest. That is why the documents matter more than the listing.

sections.h: The HOA documents decide which policy fits
p: Two townhouses can look the same from the street and be insured completely differently. What matters is how the community is legally set up and what the association agrees to insure.
Look for the insurance section of the declaration (sometimes called the CC&Rs) and the bylaws. They say whether the association insures the buildings, and if so, where its coverage stops.
If there is a master policy, ask for its declarations page. It shows what is insured, the limits and the deductibles.
Getting this wrong can leave a gap, such as no one insuring the roof, or two policies insuring the same walls.

sections.h: When you own the building: a homeowners policy
p: In many townhouse communities you own the structure and the lot, and the association insures only common areas such as the pool, clubhouse and grounds.
Then you usually need a homeowners policy, often an HO-3, for the whole building: roof, exterior walls, interior, your belongings and your liability, subject to the policy's terms.
Set the dwelling limit to what it would cost to rebuild your unit, including your share of any shared walls the documents make yours.

sections.h: When the association insures the building: a condo policy
p: Some townhouse communities are condominiums. The association insures the buildings on a master policy, and owners carry a condo policy, often an HO-6.

A condo policy can cover what the master policy leaves out, such as interior finishes, upgrades, your belongings, liability and loss of use, subject to its terms. How much you need depends on where the master policy stops.
Ask whether the master policy covers the bare walls only or also the original cabinets, floors and fixtures. See condo insurance and the HOA master policy.

sections.h: Shared walls and the units next door
p: Fire, water and wind do not stop at the property line. A loss can start in one unit and reach the next.
In general, each owner's own policy is the starting point for damage to their own home, subject to its terms. Carriers may then sort out responsibility between themselves.

Liability coverage matters more when neighbors are a wall away. Choose a limit that fits what you own, and ask about umbrella insurance if you have significant savings, subject to its terms and underwriting.

sections.h: Wind, the hurricane deductible and the HOA's deductible
p: Near the coast, wind is sometimes excluded and written separately, sometimes through the Alabama Insurance Underwriting Association. See wind insurance and the AIUA.
Most coastal policies carry a percentage hurricane or named-storm deductible. Work out what it means in dollars. See how hurricane deductibles work.

If the association insures the buildings, its master policy has its own deductible, and associations can assess owners for shared costs. Loss assessment coverage on your policy may help with your share, up to its limit.

sections.h: Flood
p: Homeowners and condo policies do not cover flood. A National Flood Insurance Program or private flood policy is a separate purchase. See flood insurance.
If the community is a condominium, the association may insure the building on an NFIP condominium association policy. Unit owners can still buy their own flood policy for their unit and belongings.
If you own your townhouse outright, flood is usually bought much like it is for a house. Your lender may require it in a high-risk flood zone. Check the FEMA flood map for the address.

sections.h: Do I need homeowners (HO-3) or condo (HO-6) insurance for a townhouse?
p: It depends on how the community is set up, not on how the building looks. If you own the structure and the lot and the association insures only common areas, a homeowners policy is usually the fit. If the community is a condominium and the association insures the building, a condo policy usually fills in the rest. The HOA's declaration and bylaws say who insures what, so read them before you choose a policy.

sections.h: Who insures the roof and outside walls of my townhouse?
p: The HOA documents decide. In some communities the association insures the roofs and exterior walls. In others each owner insures their own building, roof included. Ask the HOA for the insurance section of the declaration and the master policy declarations page, if there is one, before closing.

sections.h: If a fire in my neighbor's townhouse spreads to mine, whose policy pays?
p: In general, each owner's own policy is the starting point for damage to their own home, subject to its terms. Insurance companies may then sort out responsibility between themselves. How a specific loss is handled depends on the policies involved and the facts, so call your agent and your carrier right away if it happens.

sections.h: Can the HOA bill me for its deductible after a storm?
p: It can happen. If the association insures the buildings, a storm loss may fall under the master policy's wind or named-storm deductible, and associations can assess owners for shared costs. Loss assessment coverage on your own policy may help pay your share, up to its limit and subject to the policy's terms. Ask the HOA how its deductible would be handled.

If you own your townhouse outright, flood is usually bought much like it is for a house. A lender may require flood insurance in a high-risk flood zone.

sections.h: What makes a roof FORTIFIED
p: A FORTIFIED Roof is built or replaced to a specific standard and checked by a certified FORTIFIED evaluator. IBHS has separate designations for a new roof and for an existing roof. In general terms, the standard focuses on:
Keeping the roof deck attached with stronger nailing, so wind is less likely to peel sheathing off.
A sealed roof deck, so if shingles blow off, rain is less likely to get into the attic and the home.
Edges and openings rated for high wind, where roof damage often starts.

FORTIFIED has three levels. FORTIFIED Roof covers the roof. FORTIFIED Silver adds protection for windows, doors and other openings, and FORTIFIED Gold ties the structure together from the roof to the foundation. IBHS designs the program to help homes stand up to severe weather such as high winds, hurricanes and hail.
The certificate that comes with the designation is the document carriers ask for.

p: Under Alabama Department of Insurance rules, admitted Alabama carriers give discounts on the wind portion of the premium for homes with a FORTIFIED designation.

The size of the discount depends on the FORTIFIED level and on which of three zones the home is in. The Alabama Department of Insurance publishes a FORTIFIED discount bulletin (Bulletin 2016-07), and IBHS shows the Alabama discount zones.
A FORTIFIED roof can also widen the carriers and options available for a coastal home, depending on the carrier.

Some private carriers include wind in the homeowners policy instead of excluding it. A FORTIFIED or newer roof may help a coastal home qualify with those carriers, subject to their underwriting. sections.h: What do Alabama home insurance companies look at about a home's condition?
p: Most companies want to know the roof's age, covering and condition, along with the home's age, construction and location. Many also ask about the electrical, plumbing and heating and air systems, and some ask for photos or an inspection. Exactly what each company asks, and what it accepts, varies by company.

The Alabama Department of Insurance lists the type of construction and the age of the house among the things that affect home insurance prices, and notes that some companies may not insure very old homes or may offer a limited form of coverage. A shopping worksheet from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), posted by the Department, asks for the roof type, the approximate age of the roof and the approximate age of the plumbing, electrical, heating and air conditioning systems.

sections.h: Why do insurance companies ask how old my roof is?
p: The roof is a home's first defense against wind and rain, so its age and condition tell a company a lot about the risk. Roof age can affect whether a company offers a policy, the price, and in some policies how a roof claim is settled. Roof age guidelines vary by company.

Some policies settle roof damage on an actual cash value basis, which subtracts depreciation for age and condition. The Department's own example of depreciation is a 17-year-old roof with a 20-year warranty. Your declarations page and endorsements show how your roof is covered, subject to the policy's terms. See actual cash value in plain terms.
From Brian's inspector side: a roof can look newer or older than it is from the ground, so the year on a roofing invoice or permit is a better answer than a guess.

sections.h: What roof details should I have before I ask for a quote?
p: Have the year the roof was installed or last replaced, the covering (such as shingle or metal), the general shape, and any recent repairs. If the home has a FORTIFIED certificate, have that too. The table below shows where to find each one.
If you are not sure of the year, an estimate is a fine place to start. The NAIC worksheet notes that you can pull together what you can, and an agent may be able to help with the rest.

sections.h: Do insurance companies ask about the electrical panel, plumbing, water heater and heating and air?
p: Some do, especially on older homes. Questions can cover the electrical panel and wiring, the type and age of the plumbing, the water heater's age, and the heating and air system. Which questions a company asks, and which answers it accepts, varies by company.

From Brian's inspector side: the label inside the electrical panel door and the data labels on the water heater and the outdoor air conditioning unit often carry the manufacturer and model details that help answer age questions. A clear photo of each saves a trip back into the closet or attic later.

sections.h: What is a 4-point inspection, and will an Alabama company ask for one?
p: A 4-point inspection is a short, insurance-focused look at four parts of a home: the roof, electrical, plumbing, and heating and air. It is not a full home inspection. Some companies ask for one, or for a similar report or photos, and others do not. Whether it is required, which form is used and who may complete it vary by company.

The Alabama law and Department of Insurance guidance cited on this page do not set a standard 4-point form, so the company's own instructions are the ones to follow. If a company asks for one, ask your agent which form it wants, who may sign it and how recent it must be.

sections.h: Is a home inspection for buying the same as an insurance inspection?
p: No. A buyer's home inspection reports on the visible condition of many parts of the home for the buyer's own information. An insurance inspection answers a specific company's questions. The ASHI and InterNACHI standards both say a home inspection does not determine the insurability of the property, though the report can still help you answer a company's questions.

Alabama's standards of practice for home inspectors (Ala. Admin. Code r. 170-X-25-.01) have the inspector inspect and describe the roof covering, the water heating equipment, the electrical service and panels, and the heating and air conditioning equipment. The same rule says inspectors are not required to determine the remaining life of any system or component, which is why a receipt is still the best source for a roof's age.

sections.h: Can an insurance company inspect or photograph my home after I buy a policy?
p: Yes, some do. A company may have someone look at or photograph a home before or after a policy starts, and what they see can lead to questions or repair requests. The NAIC worksheet posted by the Alabama Department of Insurance suggests asking whether the company will inspect or photograph your home.

For wind coverage through the Alabama Insurance Underwriting Association (AIUA), photos are among the documents its closing binder requires, and its FAQ says a structure with pre-existing damage is not eligible. See wind insurance and the AIUA for how wind-only policies work.

sections.h: How does a FORTIFIED roof relate to wind premium discounts in Alabama?
p: Since 2009, Alabama law (Ala. Code 27-31D-1 and 27-31D-2) has required insurance companies to provide a premium discount or rate reduction for homes built or retrofitted to the FORTIFIED standards. The discount applies to policies that include wind coverage, either to the wind portion of the premium or to the total premium if the company does not price wind separately. The amount follows each company's filed rating plan.

The FORTIFIED certification has to be presented to the company before the discount takes effect. FORTIFIED certificates are valid for five years, and a renewal inspection by a certified FORTIFIED evaluator is required at the end of each five-year period. The Department's disaster guide adds that mitigation improvements are subject to inspection and verification by the insurer.

For the FORTIFIED levels, Strengthen Alabama Homes grants and the certificate itself, see FORTIFIED roofs explained. For how wind deductibles work, see hurricane deductibles explained. Buying a newly built home with a FORTIFIED certificate? See new construction home insurance.

sections.h: Is there a FORTIFIED option if a covered claim means a new roof?
p: Alabama law (Ala. Code 27-31D-2.1) requires companies writing homeowners insurance to offer a FORTIFIED roof endorsement. It upgrades an eligible home's roof to a FORTIFIED standard when damage covered by the policy requires the roof to be replaced. The offer is made when a new policy is written and at the first renewal after January 1, 2020. Whether you have it, and what it pays, is subject to the endorsement's terms.
If you are not sure whether your policy has this endorsement, check your declarations page or ask your agent before storm season.

sections.h: What photos and documents should I have ready?
p: Have the roof receipt or permit, current photos of the house and roof, any FORTIFIED certificate, prior inspection reports, and receipts for electrical, plumbing, water heater and heating and air work. Not every company asks for all of these, but having them ready saves back and forth.
Roof: the contract or invoice showing the install date, the permit if one was pulled, and any repair invoices.

Photos: each side of the house, the roof from the ground, the electrical panel label, the water heater label and the outdoor air conditioning unit. The Department's shopping guide notes that agents usually ask for a picture of the home.
FORTIFIED: the certificate with its ID number and date.
Reports: your home inspection report from the purchase and any later inspection or wind mitigation paperwork.

Updates: invoices for electrical, plumbing, water heater and heating and air work. Alabama's mitigation discount law also tells owners claiming certain discounts to keep construction records, including receipts from contractors and for materials.

sections.h: What if my home has damage or repairs that are not finished?
p: Tell your agent up front. Existing damage can affect whether a company will write a home, and the requirements vary by company. For example, the AIUA's FAQ says a structure with pre-existing damage is not eligible, and a home under renovation needs a licensed contractor's contract or work order for review.
Finishing known repairs before you shop, and keeping the invoices and before and after photos, gives a company clear answers. For help after a storm, see the storm recovery guide.

sections.h: What FORTIFIED Gold means for a new home
p: FORTIFIED is a construction standard from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety (IBHS). It has three levels, and each one includes the one before it:
FORTIFIED Roof: stronger roof deck nailing, a sealed roof deck, locked-down roof edges and wind-rated vents.
FORTIFIED Silver: adds protection for windows, doors, garage doors, gable ends, soffits and attached porches.
FORTIFIED Gold: adds an engineered continuous load path, so the roof, walls and foundation are tied together as one structure.

A certified FORTIFIED evaluator checks the work during construction, and IBHS issues a certificate to the property address with a FORTIFIED ID number. On new construction, the designation is valid for five years, and the home can be re-designated for another five years after an evaluator's inspection.

Under Alabama Department of Insurance rules, admitted Alabama carriers give discounts on the wind portion of the premium for homes with a FORTIFIED designation at any of the three levels: Roof, Silver or Gold. We submit the certificate for whichever level your home earned. FORTIFIED Gold earns the largest discount of the three, so a new home that meets the Gold standard and receives its Gold certificate qualifies for the Gold-level wind discount. The size of the discount depends on the level and the home's zone, and the Department publishes a FORTIFIED discount bulletin (Bulletin 2016-07), and IBHS shows the Alabama discount zones.

sections.h: What a boat policy usually includes
p: Personal watercraft and fishing boats. Jet skis, pontoons, bay boats, sailboats and center consoles can usually be written on a boat insurance policy. Some carriers write personal watercraft separately.
Physical damage. Hull, motor and equipment, valued either at an agreed value set when the policy starts or at actual cash value, which subtracts depreciation.
Liability. Injuries to others and damage to other boats, docks or property, subject to the policy's limits and terms.
Medical payments and uninsured boater coverage, where offered.
Trailer, towing and assistance, and in some policies fuel spill liability and wreck removal.
Coverages are different from one carrier to the next. Compare what each policy covers rather than the price alone.

sections.h: Agreed value or actual cash value
p: Agreed value means the boat's value for a total loss is set when the policy is written. Actual cash value subtracts depreciation at the time of the loss.
Ask which type of valuation a quote uses, since it changes what a total loss pays.

sections.h: Navigation limits
p: Policies describe where the boat may be used, such as inland waters, Mobile Bay or a set distance offshore in the Gulf.

sections.h: Liability and the rest of your coverage
p: Docks and lifts at your home may fall under the homeowners policy or need separate coverage. An umbrella policy can add liability above the boat policy if the umbrella lists it.

sections.h: How a boat insurance claim works

sections.h: What is the difference between agreed value and actual cash value on a boat policy?

sections.h: Home: protect your pipes before sunset
p: Disconnect and drain garden hoses. Put insulated covers on outdoor faucets. If your outdoor faucets have indoor shutoff valves, close those valves and open the outdoor faucets to drain the remaining water. Follow your system's instructions for winterizing irrigation lines and backflow devices.
Insulate exposed water pipes. Check crawl spaces, garages and the underside of raised homes. Foam pipe sleeves are a simple way to protect accessible pipes in unheated areas.

Keep heat near vulnerable plumbing. Leave the heat on and keep the garage door closed if water lines run through it. During a hard freeze, open sink cabinet doors along exterior walls so warm air can circulate, and move cleaners out of reach of children and pets. Follow your water utility's guidance on whether to leave a vulnerable faucet trickling.

Find your main water shutoff now. Make sure everyone in the household knows where it is. If a pipe bursts, shut off the water if you can safely reach the valve and call a plumber. See the American Red Cross guide to frozen pipes.

sections.h: Auto: check the car and the roads
p: Check tire pressure while the tires are cold. Use the pressure listed on the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual, and look for worn tread while you're there.

Test the battery, wipers and defroster. If the engine has been slow to start, get the battery tested before the cold snap. Have your coolant checked, top off with freeze-rated windshield washer fluid, and put an ice scraper in the car.

Pack for a delay and check road conditions. Keep a blanket, flashlight and phone charger handy. If freezing rain is forecast or roads are icy, postpone trips that can wait. Bridges and overpasses can ice up before nearby roads. See NHTSA winter driving tips and NOAA winter driving hazards.

sections.h: Plants: move the pots and cover tender plants
p: Bring sensitive potted plants indoors or into a garage that stays above freezing. Start with tropicals, tender herbs and young potted citrus. Container roots are especially exposed to the cold.

Cover tender plants before sunset. Use frost cloth or an old sheet. Drape it all the way to the ground and secure the edges so it traps warmth from the soil. Use stakes to support the cover over delicate plants, and keep plastic from touching the leaves.

Uncover plants once temperatures rise above freezing. Let them get daylight and air, then cover them again before sunset if another freeze is on the way. If shrubs look damaged afterward, wait until the risk of another freeze passes before pruning. See the Alabama Extension guides to frost protection and post-freeze plant care.

sections.h: Where the Beach Pool fits
p: On the Alabama coast, a home's wind coverage usually ends up one of three ways:
One policy with wind included. A private carrier writes the homeowners policy with wind and hail included, subject to its terms.
Homeowners without wind, plus a private wind policy. The homeowners policy excludes wind, and a private carrier writes wind separately.
Homeowners without wind, plus the Beach Pool. When the regular market will not write wind, the AIUA may.
Flood is separate in all three. For how the pieces fit together, see wind insurance in Baldwin County.

sections.h: Check for a policy with wind included first
p: Not every coastal home needs the Beach Pool. Some private carriers include wind in the homeowners policy instead of excluding it, so the home has one policy for wind, other covered causes of loss and liability.
Brian works with carriers that build wind into their homeowners policies. Whether a particular home qualifies depends on the carrier's underwriting, including the roof, construction and location.
If a private carrier will not write wind for the home, the Beach Pool is the fallback. That is the role it was created for.

sections.h: Who is eligible
p: The AIUA covers eligible properties south of the 31st parallel in Baldwin and Mobile counties. The AIUA website has a map tool to check an address.
The AIUA does not insure vacant or farm property, structures with pre-existing damage, or property in areas protected by the federal Coastal Barrier Resources Act.
A home under renovation may be eligible if the work is documented by a licensed contractor and meets the AIUA's conditions, which include an owner-occupied dwelling.
Mobile and manufactured homes have their own requirements, such as tie-downs and a current installation label.

sections.h: How you apply
p: You cannot apply to the AIUA directly. Applications go through an AIUA authorized agent.
The agent completes prescreening questions, but the AIUA decides whether the property meets its standards, and agents cannot bind coverage on its behalf.

For a home purchase with a new mortgage, the AIUA describes a 30-day closing binder that requires the application, photos, closing documents and payment before the binder expires. Ask your agent about timing early.
AIUA policies do not renew automatically. The AIUA sends an offer to rewrite coverage before the policy expires, so watch for it.

sections.h: What a Beach Pool policy does and doesn't include
p: The AIUA requires a home to be insured to 100% of its value, up to maximum dwelling and personal property limits that it publishes in its frequently asked questions. The AIUA raised those limits on November 1, 2025. If a home is worth more than the maximum, ask how the rest of its value would be covered.
The AIUA does not offer liability coverage or loss assessment coverage. Those come from another policy, such as an ex-wind homeowners or condo policy.
AIUA policies include limited fair rental value coverage, as described in the policy form.

Hurricane deductibles are a percentage. When a home is worth more than the AIUA's maximum limit, the AIUA bases the percentage deductible on the structure's total insurable value, not the limit. See how hurricane deductibles work.
FORTIFIED discounts apply to policies that provide wind coverage under Alabama law, and the AIUA's policy outline shows which discounts were applied. See FORTIFIED roofs.

sections.h: Flood and the Beach Pool
p: For properties in flood zones A or V, the AIUA requires flood coverage at least equal to the AIUA policy limits or the most the National Flood Insurance Program offers.
Condo owners in those zones must carry their own flood policy even if the association insures the building for flood, unless the unit is above the second level of a multi-level building.
Flood is never part of the Beach Pool policy itself. See flood insurance.

sections.h: Timing and storms
p: The AIUA closes to new business applications and binders when a named storm is inside a set area of the Gulf and Atlantic or a tropical storm watch or warning is issued for Baldwin or Mobile county. It reopens 24 hours after the storm dissipates and all watches and warnings are lifted.
Many private carriers also pause new policies while a storm threatens the coast, so settle wind coverage well before storm season.

faqs.q: Is there a maximum amount the Beach Pool will insure?
faqs.a: Yes. The AIUA requires a home to be insured to 100% of its value, up to maximum dwelling and personal property limits that the AIUA sets and publishes in its frequently asked questions. The AIUA raised those limits on November 1, 2025. If your home is worth more than the maximum, ask your agent how the rest of its value would be covered.

faqs.q: Does the Beach Pool require flood insurance?
faqs.a: For properties in flood zones A or V, yes. The AIUA requires flood coverage at least equal to the AIUA policy limits or the maximum available from the National Flood Insurance Program. Condo owners must also carry their own flood policy unless the unit is above the second level of a multi-level building, according to the AIUA.

faqs.q: Can I get a Beach Pool policy when a storm is coming?
faqs.a: Usually not. The AIUA says it closes to new business applications and binders when a named storm is inside a set area of the Gulf and Atlantic or a tropical storm watch or warning is issued for Baldwin or Mobile county, until 24 hours after the storm dissipates and watches and warnings are lifted. Plan ahead of storm season.

p: Prepared by Brian Lehmann, licensed Alabama insurance agent, Alabama Coastal Insurance in Fairhope. Updated November 21, 2026.
For pickup owners in Fairhope, Daphne, Spanish Fort, Foley, Robertsdale, Gulf Shores and the rest of Baldwin County, from weekend boat haulers to tradespeople who drive their own trucks to work.
Licensed Alabama agent in Fairhope. Tell Brian how you use your truck and what you tow, and he will help you find coverage that fits.

sections.h: Why trucks raise different questions
p: A pickup is often a personal vehicle, a work vehicle and a tow vehicle all at once. Each of those uses can touch a different policy:
Personal driving. Usually a personal auto policy, the same as a car.
Work use. Depending on how the truck is used and owned, it may need commercial auto insurance.
Towing. The truck's policy, the boat or camper's own policy, and sometimes the trailer each have a role.
Commercial trucking (box trucks, haulers and fleets) is a different kind of policy. See business insurance.

sections.h: Personal use or business use
p: A personal auto policy is written for personal driving. Driving your pickup to a job site is usually personal use.

Hauling equipment for customers, carrying a crew, delivering for pay or pulling a work trailer is different. Many personal policies limit or exclude certain business uses, and where the line falls depends on the carrier and the policy's terms.
Ownership matters too. If the truck is titled to your business or the business pays for it, that often points to a commercial auto policy.
Tell your agent exactly how you use the truck. That is the simplest way to avoid a gap.

sections.h: Company trucks and delivery apps
p: Driving a truck your employer provides? Many personal auto policies exclude vehicles furnished for your regular use, so a company truck you take home is usually covered, if at all, by the employer's policy. Ask your employer whether personal use is allowed and covered.
Some carriers offer an endorsement that can extend your own liability coverage to a vehicle furnished for your regular use.

Delivering food or packages for an app in your own truck? Many personal policies limit coverage while you deliver for pay. Some carriers offer a delivery or rideshare endorsement, subject to its terms.

sections.h: Towing a boat, camper or trailer
p: Your truck's auto policy often extends liability to a trailer while it is hitched to the truck, subject to the policy's terms.
Damage to the boat or camper itself usually comes from its own policy. See boat insurance and RV insurance.
Some boat policies include the trailer and some do not, so ask.
Once a camper is unhitched and set up at a campsite, the truck's policy usually isn't the one covering it.

sections.h: Lift kits, upgrades and tools in the bed
p: Many personal auto policies include only a limited amount for parts and equipment that didn't come from the factory, such as lift kits, wheels, light bars and bed covers. Custom parts and equipment coverage may be available for more, subject to the policy's terms.
Keep a list of every upgrade with receipts and photos, and tell your agent when you add something significant. A lift can also change how a carrier looks at the truck.
Tools and equipment you use for work are usually a separate business question. Ask your agent how they're covered.

sections.h: What Alabama requires, and what lenders add
p: Alabama law requires liability insurance to operate or keep registered a motor vehicle designed for public roads, and a pickup is no exception. The minimum limits are the same for a truck as for a car. See auto insurance in Alabama.
Liability pays others when you are at fault. It does not repair your truck or pay your own medical bills.
Uninsured motorist coverage must be offered with an Alabama policy, and the named insured has the right to reject it. Ask whether yours has it.
If the truck is financed or leased, the lender will usually require collision and comprehensive.

sections.h: Hurricanes, flood and falling trees
p: Storm damage to a truck, including flood and falling trees, falls under comprehensive coverage, subject to the policy's terms and deductible.
Comprehensive is optional unless a lender requires it, so a truck with liability only has no coverage for its own storm damage.
Before a storm, move the truck to higher ground if you can. Flood damage to vehicles is common on the coast.

sections.h: Questions to answer before you quote your truck
p: Do you ever use it to haul for pay, carry a crew or make deliveries?
Is it titled to you or to a business, and who pays for it?
What do you tow: a boat, a camper, a work or utility trailer?
What have you added: a lift, wheels, a light bar, a toolbox?
Do you want comprehensive for storm and flood damage?

sections.h: Does my personal auto policy cover my pickup if I use it for work?
p: It depends on how you use it. Driving to and from a job is usually personal use. Hauling equipment for customers, carrying a crew or delivering for pay is different, and many personal auto policies limit or exclude certain business uses. Where the line falls depends on the carrier and the policy's terms, so tell your agent exactly how you use the truck.

sections.h: Do I need commercial auto insurance for my truck?
p: You may, if the truck is owned by or titled to a business, the business pays for it, or it is used mainly for work such as hauling tools, making deliveries or carrying clients. Commercial auto insurance is written for business vehicles. An agent can look at how the truck is owned and used and tell you which kind of policy fits.

sections.h: Does my truck insurance cover the boat or camper I tow?
p: Partly. Auto policies often extend liability to a trailer while it is hitched to the insured vehicle. Damage to the boat or camper itself usually comes from that boat or camper's own policy, and some boat policies include the trailer while others do not. Once a camper is unhitched at a campsite, its own policy is usually the one that applies.

sections.h: Are lift kits, wheels and other aftermarket parts covered?
p: Often only up to a limited amount. Many personal auto policies include a small amount for parts and equipment that did not come from the factory. Custom parts and equipment coverage may be available for the rest, subject to the policy's terms. Keep receipts and photos, and tell your agent when you add something significant.

sections.h: Are the tools in my truck bed covered?
p: Usually not by a personal auto policy, which is built for the vehicle. Tools you use for work are generally a business question, often handled with a separate policy for tools and equipment. Personal belongings in the truck may fall under a homeowners or renters policy, subject to its limits. Ask your agent how your tools are covered.

sections.h: Does truck insurance cover hurricane, flood or falling-tree damage?
p: That is comprehensive coverage, which is optional unless a lender requires it. The Insurance Information Institute lists fire, flood, hail and falling trees among the things comprehensive covers. Without comprehensive, a policy with liability only does not pay to repair or replace your own truck.

sections.h: Alabama motorcycle insurance requirements
p: Liability insurance is required before a bike, like any motor vehicle, can be registered and ridden on public roads. The minimum limits are 25/50/25, the same as a car.
Proof of insurance is needed to register the bike. You may be asked for it at a traffic stop. Keep it with you when you ride.

Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage must be offered with the policy. You can reject it or choose lower limits. Carriers often ask you to sign a form to do that. It matters to riders. A crash with an uninsured driver can leave you with large injury bills.
A lender will often require collision and comprehensive on a financed bike.

sections.h: Motorcycle insurance coverages to compare
p: Liability coverage for injuries and property damage you cause to others in a crash.
Collision for crash damage to your bike. Comprehensive coverage for other damage, including theft, fire, vandalism, hail, falling trees and flood.
Medical payments coverage for your own injuries and your passenger's after a crash, no matter who is at fault. It depends on the carrier.
Roadside assistance and trip interruption coverage, depending on the carrier.
Do you use the bike for deliveries or other paid work? A personal policy may exclude that use. Ask about commercial coverage. See business insurance.

sections.h: Custom parts, gear and total loss
p: Chrome, custom paint, saddlebags, upgraded seats and electronics may need their own custom parts and equipment coverage. A standard policy may pay only a small amount for them.
Some carriers cover riding gear, such as helmets and jackets, damaged in a covered crash.
Ask how a total loss is paid: actual cash value, agreed value or replacement for a newer bike.

sections.h: Storage and hurricane season
p: Tell your agent where the bike is kept. A locked garage, a carport or a coastal condo lot can change the options.
Comprehensive is what often applies to storm, flood and falling-tree damage. Ask before hurricane season whether your policy includes it. See the hurricane preparedness checklist.
Do you only ride part of the year? Ask whether the carrier offers a lay-up or storage option.

sections.h: Motorcycle insurance discounts
p: Many carriers offer motorcycle insurance discounts for a safety course. One example is a course approved by the Motorcycle Safety Foundation.
Bundling your bike with your car or home insurance can help you save on the total cost. It depends on the carrier. See Alabama auto insurance.
Insuring more than one bike can also help. So can an anti-theft device and a clean riding record.
Your age, riding experience, the type of bike and where you live also affect your costs.
An umbrella policy can add liability above your bike and auto policies if it lists them.

sections.h: Filing a motorcycle insurance claim
p: After a crash, theft or storm, make sure everyone is safe. Then take photos and report the claim to the carrier as soon as you can.
Keep receipts for towing, medical care and repairs. Take reasonable steps to protect the bike from further damage.
Whether claims are paid, and how much, depends on the policy's terms, deductibles and exclusions.

sections.h: Questions to ask about Baldwin County motorcycle insurance
p: Do my liability limits go beyond the state minimum?
Does my policy include uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage?
Is there medical payments coverage for me and a passenger?
What does the policy pay for a total loss: actual cash value, agreed value or replacement?
Is comprehensive on the policy for hurricane season?

sections.h: Is motorcycle insurance required in Alabama?
p: Yes. Liability insurance in Alabama is required for motorcycles. The minimum limits are the same as a car, written as 25/50/25. Those numbers are in thousands of dollars: bodily injury per person, bodily injury per accident, and property damage. Your lender may also require collision and comprehensive on a financed bike.

sections.h: Does my car insurance cover my motorcycle?
p: Usually not. A bike needs its own policy, or its own listing on a policy that allows motorcycles. Many carriers can bundle the two.

sections.h: Does Alabama require a motorcycle helmet?
p: Yes. State law requires every rider and passenger to wear a helmet. Some carriers offer riding gear coverage. It can help replace a helmet damaged in a covered crash.

sections.h: Can a safety course lower my motorcycle insurance?
p: It can. Many carriers offer a discount for an approved safety course. Ask your agent which courses each carrier accepts.
